performers: Adèle Bérard, soprano; Laura Lazayre, piano (duo Béla)
intro: Eight of the sixteen lines of Heine’s Warum sind denn die Rosen so blass begin with “Warum”, and Fanny Hensel sets its four stanzas to two melodies, each heard twice. Adèle Bérard (soprano) and Laura Lazayre (piano), who perform as duo Béla, recorded the song in Amiens in January 2026.

cues.title: Composed 1837, published 1846
cues.text: Hensel wrote this song in 1837. It appeared in 1846 as No. 3 of her Sechs Lieder, Op. 1, from Bote & Bock in Berlin. On 9 July of that year she told her brother Felix, who had opposed her publishing, that she had accepted Herr Bock’s terms.
cues.evidence: IMSLP lists the song as Op. 1, No. 3 (H.312) in Sechs Lieder, first published by Bote & Bock, Berlin, in 1846 (plate B. et B. 1046; title page of IMSLP #99178). The Naxos 8.570981 booklet and LiederNet date it 1837, as does the chronological list of her works after Hellwig-Unruh’s catalogue (H-U 312). Hensel to Felix, 22 November 1836 (“Hensel wünscht es, Du bist dagegen”, “Hensel wants it, you are against it”) and 9 July 1846 (“ich fange an herauszugeben”, “I am beginning to publish”, after giving Herr Bock’s offer and terms a favourable hearing): https://fannyhensel.de/?page_id=138 https://imslp.org/wiki/Warum_sind_denn_die_Rosen_so_blass,_H.312_(Hensel,_Fanny) https://stor.imslp.org/naxos/booklets/booklet-8.570981.pdf https://www.lieder.net/lieder/get_text.html?TextId=7780 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_compositions_by_Fanny_Hensel

cues.title: Second stanza in D minor
cues.text: The second stanza starts marked f, in D minor, with a stepwise descent in the voice and running sixteenths in the piano. Near its end the left hand holds E for two bars, a dominant pedal. The first stanza’s melody then returns for the third stanza.
cues.evidence: Bote & Bock first edition (IMSLP #99178), pp. 9–10: f at the entry of the second stanza, with B♭ in the voice and piano and the left hand beginning D, E, C, F; the left hand holds E for two bars at the end of the first system and the start of the second system of p. 10; the third stanza then opens with the music of the first (p. 10, second system). https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/24/IMSLP99178-PMLP194743-Hensel_Fanny_Sechs_Lieder_fuer_eine_Stimme_mit_Begleitung_des_Pianoforte_Op_1_Bote_1046_1846.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Last line repeated, piano close
cues.text: After the fourth stanza Hensel repeats the last line, with “warum” sung twice. The soprano sings the melody of the opening line, marked con espress. The piano then plays alone, dim. and rallent., and finishes pp on an A minor arpeggio rising to a high A under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Bote & Bock first edition (IMSLP #99178), p. 11, systems 3–4: “Warum, warum verliessest du mich?” marked con espress., to the music of the opening line on p. 9; the piano bars after it are marked dim. rallent. and pp and end on a high A with a fermata. Heine’s text has the line once (LiederNet, after Buch der Lieder, 1827, p. 129: https://www.lieder.net/lieder/get_text.html?TextId=7780). https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/24/IMSLP99178-PMLP194743-Hensel_Fanny_Sechs_Lieder_fuer_eine_Stimme_mit_Begleitung_des_Pianoforte_Op_1_Bote_1046_1846.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Commons description lists duo Béla with Adèle Bérard, soprano, and Laura Lazayre, piano. The ICCARE programme lists the same duo’s recital with the pianist’s surname spelt Lazayres; no other source for the spelling was found, and the Commons spelling, which appears on all three files the uploader posted, is kept. The file is credited to the uploader Magiraud as own work; the page does not name the uploader as a performer.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Complete song as printed in Op. 1 No. 3, sung in the printed key (A minor), with the repeat of the last line
fields.note: The Commons title and description identify the song, and the page links the OpenScore Lieder project as the score; its transcription of this song is a CC0 encoding made from the Bote & Bock first edition (IMSLP #99178). That the performance is complete, untransposed and follows the printed repeat is estimated from the audio and the printed score: the piano’s opening E5 measures 659.6 Hz, the soprano’s first notes sound as A4 and E5, the closing chord is A minor, and audio chroma aligned with the encoded score follows four stanzas in printed order and then the repeated last line. Tuning is about A = 440 Hz. The sung words were not transcribed. IMSLP gives the key as A minor and the first edition marks the song Andante (p. 9). The Naxos booklet, LiederNet and the chronological work list after Hellwig-Unruh’s catalogue date the song 1837; IMSLP and the first edition place its publication in 1846, the year Hensel told her brother Felix that she had accepted Herr Bock’s offer (letter of 9 July 1846).

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Commons date field gives 2026-01-22, and the ICCARE programme places the duo’s recital, billed “avec captation libre”, on Thursday 22 January from 18:00 to 19:00. The Commons description gives 22–23 January, the span of the conference days. The page does not say whether the file records the public recital or another run-through on the same day. The upload timestamp, 23 January 2026 at 09:08 UTC, is not a session date.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain: Hensel died in 1847 and Heine in 1856, and the first edition appeared in 1846.
fields.note: Life-plus-70 terms have run out for both authors, and IMSLP lists the 1846 Bote & Bock edition as public domain. This covers the song and its text, not modern editions; the OpenScore Lieder transcription is released under CC0.

The licence is the uploader’s own-work declaration, and the Commons page carries no separate statement or permission ticket from the performers. The ICCARE programme, which announces the recital as “avec captation libre” at a conference on open licences and open data, points to an open release but gives no licence terms. composer.epithet: Berlin composer who ran the city’s Sunday concerts, wrote more than 450 works and published collections under her own name only in the last year of her life.
facts: Ludwig Berger, piano; Carl Friedrich Zelter, composition
Sunday concerts at Leipziger Straße 3, Berlin; pianist, conductor and organiser
Married the painter Wilhelm Hensel in 1829; son Sebastian born in 1830
More than 450 works; songs, piano music, chamber music, cantatas and an overture
composer.background:
On 9 July 1846 Fanny Hensel wrote to her brother Felix with news she expected him to dislike. A Berlin publisher had offered good terms for her songs, and she had accepted. “In a word, I am beginning to publish,” she wrote, after a long and uneasy preamble about her wish to please the people she loved. She was forty. She had been composing since childhood and directed some of Berlin’s most distinguished private concerts.

Born in Hamburg on 14 November 1805, Fanny was the eldest child of the banker Abraham Mendelssohn and his wife Lea. The family moved to Berlin in 1811. Her grandfather was the philosopher Moses Mendelssohn, an advocate of Jewish civil equality; Abraham and Lea had their four children baptised as Protestants in 1816, and later added Bartholdy to the family name. Fanny’s first piano teacher was her mother. As a child she learnt all twenty-four preludes of the first book of Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier by heart and played them to her father.
